docs.title: ISO 27001 Readiness & Implementation
docs.text: ISO 27001 readiness and implementation: scope, risk assessment, ISMS, Statement of Applicability, internal audit and support through independent certification.

docs.title: How long does ISO 27001 take?
docs.text: It depends on the scope, your existing controls, how quickly evidence of operation can be built up and the certification body's availability. We set out a realistic plan once we understand your starting position, rather than quoting a standard timescale.

docs.title: Do you issue the ISO 27001 certificate?
docs.text: No. Certificates are issued by independent certification bodies, which should be accredited by a recognised accreditation body such as UKAS in the United Kingdom. We prepare you for their audit and support you through it.

docs.title: Do we need ISO 27001 or Cyber Essentials?
docs.text: They meet different needs. Cyber Essentials is a UK scheme covering a defined set of technical controls. ISO 27001 is an international management system standard covering governance, risk and a much broader set of controls. The right answer depends on what your customers or contracts require.

docs.title: Do we need a technical team to achieve ISO 27001?
docs.text: ISO 27001 is a management system standard, so leadership involvement and clear ownership matter as much as technical skill. Technical controls still need to be implemented, and we work with your team or suppliers to do that.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Agreeing which parts of the organisation, locations, systems and services the ISMS will cover, and recording the boundaries clearly.

docs.title: Gap assessment
docs.text: Reviewing current practice against the clauses of the standard and the Annex A controls to establish where work is needed.

docs.title: Risk assessment and treatment
docs.text: Establishing a risk methodology, identifying information security risks and deciding how each will be treated.

docs.title: Statement of Applicability
docs.text: Recording which Annex A controls apply, why, and how they are implemented, with justified exclusions.

docs.title: Policies and controls
docs.text: Developing the policies, procedures and technical and organisational controls the risk assessment calls for, sized to the organisation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Establishing records that show controls are operating, so an auditor can test practice rather than documents alone.

docs.title: Awareness
docs.text: Helping staff understand their responsibilities under the ISMS through proportionate awareness activity.

docs.title: Internal audit
docs.text: Planning and conducting an internal audit so that nonconformities are identified and addressed before the certification audit.

docs.title: Management review and corrective action
docs.text: Supporting leadership through management review, and establishing a corrective action process that the auditor will expect to see used.

docs.title: Certification body preparation
docs.text: Helping you select and engage an accredited certification body, preparing for Stage 1 and Stage 2, and supporting any findings through to closure.

docs.title: AI Governance & ISO 42001
docs.text: AI governance frameworks, AI inventories, risk and impact assessment, NIST AI RMF alignment and ISO 42001 readiness for independent certification.

docs.title: Is ISO 42001 mandatory?
docs.text: No. ISO/IEC 42001 is a voluntary standard. Some customers ask for it, and it can support evidence of good governance under regulatory regimes, but holding it does not in itself demonstrate compliance with any specific law.

docs.title: Does ISO 42001 make us compliant with the EU AI Act?
docs.text: Not on its own. The EU AI Act sets legal obligations that depend on the role you play and the risk category of the system. An AI management system can support those obligations, but Act-specific requirements must be addressed separately.

docs.title: We only use AI tools from suppliers. Does this apply to us?
docs.text: Often, yes. Organisations that deploy third-party AI still need to understand how it is used, what data it processes and who is accountable. The work is usually lighter than for organisations that develop AI systems.

docs.title: Governance structure
docs.text: Establishing where AI decisions are made, how they are escalated and how oversight is reported to leadership.

docs.title: Roles and accountability
docs.text: Assigning ownership for AI systems, risk decisions and monitoring, including where responsibilities sit with suppliers.

docs.title: AI inventory
docs.text: Recording the AI systems the organisation develops, deploys or relies on, and their purpose, data and users.

docs.title: Risk and impact assessment
docs.text: Assessing risks to the organisation and impacts on individuals and groups, and deciding how each will be treated.

docs.title: Lifecycle governance
docs.text: Setting controls for design, data, testing, deployment, change and retirement of AI systems.

docs.title: Third-party AI
docs.text: Assessing AI provided by suppliers or embedded in products you buy, and setting proportionate contractual and operational controls.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Aligning AI governance with data protection obligations, including impact assessments where personal data is involved.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Defining how performance, incidents and changes in risk are monitored once systems are in use.

docs.title: Policies and evidence
docs.text: Developing the policies and records that show governance is operating in practice.

docs.title: ISO 42001 readiness
docs.text: Where certification is sought, preparing the AIMS for audit by an independent certification body.

docs.title: SOC 2 Readiness
docs.text: SOC 2 readiness: scope, Trust Services Criteria, control design, evidence and Type 1 or Type 2 preparation. The examination is performed by a licensed CPA firm.

docs.title: Is SOC 2 a certification?
docs.text: No. SOC 2 is an examination performed by a licensed CPA firm, resulting in a report on your controls rather than a certificate. A consultancy cannot issue a SOC 2 report.

docs.title: Should we start with Type 1 or Type 2?
docs.text: It depends on what your customers need and when. A Type 1 report can be produced sooner and demonstrates control design. Most customers eventually expect a Type 2 report, which requires controls to operate over an examination period.

docs.title: Can one programme support SOC 2 and ISO 27001?
docs.text: Yes. The frameworks differ in structure and outcome, but many controls overlap. Designing controls and evidence once, then mapping them to both, avoids duplicated work.

docs.title: Readiness assessment
docs.text: Reviewing current controls against the Trust Services Criteria and identifying gaps.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Deciding which systems, services and criteria the report should cover, starting with Security and adding Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity or Privacy where customers need them.

docs.title: Control design
docs.text: Designing controls that meet the criteria and reflect how your organisation actually operates.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Putting controls into operation across people, process and technology, working with your team and suppliers.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Establishing how each control will be evidenced, and checking that evidence is complete and consistent.

docs.title: Type 1 and Type 2 readiness
docs.text: Preparing for a point-in-time examination, an examination over a period, or a Type 1 followed by Type 2.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Addressing gaps identified during readiness work before the examination period starts.

docs.title: Audit coordination
docs.text: Supporting you in selecting a CPA firm and coordinating information requests during the examination.

docs.title: Ongoing control maintenance
docs.text: Keeping controls and evidence operating between examinations, since Type 2 reports are usually renewed annually.

docs.title: Integration with ISO 27001
docs.text: Where you also hold or are pursuing ISO 27001, mapping controls so that one set of evidence supports both.

docs.title: Cyber Assurance & Testing
docs.text: Vulnerability assessment, web application, API, network and cloud testing, penetration testing and remediation validation, delivered by qualified testers.

docs.title: How often should we test?
docs.text: It depends on how often your systems change, your risk profile and what customers or frameworks expect. Many organisations test at least annually and after significant changes.

docs.title: Will testing disrupt our live systems?
docs.text: Testing is planned to minimise disruption, with rules of engagement agreed in advance. Some tests can be run against staging environments where they reflect production.

docs.title: Can you provide testing by an accredited provider?
docs.text: Where a customer or regulator specifies a particular accreditation for testers or testing companies, we arrange delivery through a provider that holds it and confirm this in writing before testing begins.

docs.title: Vulnerability assessment
docs.text: Identifying known weaknesses across infrastructure and applications, prioritised by risk.

docs.title: Web application testing
docs.text: Testing applications for common and business-logic weaknesses, including authentication and access control.

docs.title: API testing
docs.text: Testing APIs for weaknesses in authentication, authorisation, input handling and data exposure.

docs.title: Network testing
docs.text: Testing external and internal network exposure and segmentation.

docs.title: Cloud configuration review
docs.text: Reviewing cloud accounts and services against recognised secure configuration guidance.

docs.title: Penetration testing
docs.text: Scenario-based testing within agreed rules of engagement, to show how weaknesses could be combined.

docs.title: Remediation validation
docs.text: Retesting after fixes to confirm that findings have been addressed.

docs.title: Security assurance support
docs.text: Helping you present testing evidence to customers, auditors and insurers.

docs.title: Privacy & Data Governance
docs.text: Privacy programmes for UK GDPR, US state privacy requirements and GCC data protection laws, including DPIAs, records of processing and DPO support.

docs.title: Do we need a data protection officer?
docs.text: Under UK GDPR, a data protection officer is required for public authorities and for organisations whose core activities involve large-scale regular and systematic monitoring or large-scale processing of special category data. Other organisations may still benefit from dedicated privacy leadership.

docs.title: Is there such a thing as GDPR certification?
docs.text: Organisations are not certified as GDPR compliant by regulators. Certification schemes exist under the legislation, and ISO/IEC 27701 can be certified independently, but neither replaces the obligation to comply with the law.

docs.title: Can you help with privacy in more than one country?
docs.text: Yes. We organise the work around the regimes that apply, and assign practitioners with the relevant jurisdictional knowledge.

docs.title: Privacy assessment
docs.text: Reviewing current practice against the requirements that apply to your organisation.

docs.title: Data mapping and records
docs.text: Establishing what personal data you hold, where it flows and why, including records of processing where required.

docs.title: Impact assessments
docs.text: Conducting and reviewing data protection impact assessments and similar risk assessments.

docs.title: Policies and notices
docs.text: Developing privacy notices, policies and procedures that reflect what you actually do.

docs.title: Individual rights
docs.text: Establishing processes to handle access, deletion and other requests within the required periods.

docs.title: Breach governance
docs.text: Preparing for personal data breaches, including assessment, escalation and notification decisions.

docs.title: International transfers
docs.text: Identifying transfers and putting appropriate transfer mechanisms and safeguards in place.

docs.title: Data protection officer support
docs.text: Providing ongoing privacy leadership, including an external data protection officer service where that is appropriate for your organisation.

docs.title: vCISO & GRC Advisory
docs.text: Flexible senior security leadership and GRC advisory: strategy, risk, board reporting, customer assurance, third-party risk and ongoing ISO and SOC support.

docs.title: How is a vCISO different from a consultancy project?
docs.text: A project delivers a defined outcome and ends. A vCISO engagement provides continuing senior involvement, working with leadership over time on strategy, risk and assurance.

docs.title: Can we change the level of involvement?
docs.text: Yes. The level of involvement is agreed at the start and can be reviewed as your needs change.

docs.title: We are already certified. How does ongoing GRC support help?
docs.text: Surveillance audits test whether the management system is operating. Ongoing support keeps risk reviews, evidence, internal audit and management review current between assessments.

docs.title: Security strategy
docs.text: Setting security priorities that reflect the business, its risks and its customers.

docs.title: Risk
docs.text: Maintaining a risk register and helping leadership make and record risk decisions.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Establishing security governance, roles and reporting lines.

docs.title: Board reporting
docs.text: Reporting security posture and risk to the board in terms it can act on.

docs.title: Customer assurance
docs.text: Supporting customer due diligence, including security questionnaires and assurance meetings.

docs.title: Third-party risk
docs.text: Assessing and managing the security of suppliers and service providers.

docs.title: ISO and SOC programmes
docs.text: Overseeing ISO 27001, ISO 42001 or SOC 2 programmes and keeping them operating between audits.

docs.title: NIST alignment
docs.text: Aligning security governance to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 where that is the expected reference point.

docs.title: Regulatory readiness
docs.text: Helping the organisation prepare for regulatory requirements in its sector and jurisdiction.

docs.title: Ongoing GRC support
docs.text: Evidence and policy maintenance, internal review, management review and preparation for surveillance or recertification audits.

docs.title: Business Continuity & ISO 22301
docs.text: Business impact analysis, continuity strategy, incident response, disaster recovery, exercising and ISO 22301 readiness for independent certification.

docs.title: What is the difference between ISO 22301 and ISO 27001?
docs.text: ISO 27001 addresses information security management. ISO 22301 addresses the ability to continue operating during and after disruption. They are complementary and can share management system processes.

docs.title: Do we need certification?
docs.text: Not always. Many organisations need tested continuity arrangements to satisfy customers or regulators without pursuing certification. We help you decide which is appropriate.

docs.title: Business impact analysis
docs.text: Identifying critical activities, their dependencies and how long each can be disrupted.

docs.title: Risk assessment
docs.text: Assessing the threats most likely to disrupt critical activities.

docs.title: Continuity strategy
docs.text: Deciding how critical activities will be maintained or recovered.

docs.title: Incident response
docs.text: Establishing how incidents are escalated, managed and communicated.

docs.title: Disaster recovery
docs.text: Planning the recovery of technology and data within agreed objectives.

docs.title: Exercising and testing
docs.text: Testing plans through exercises and improving them based on what is learned.

docs.title: ISO 22301 readiness
docs.text: Where certification is sought, preparing the BCMS for audit by an independent certification body.

docs.title: Regulatory resilience requirements
docs.text: Aligning with operational resilience requirements where your regulator sets them.

docs.title: GCC Cyber & Regulatory Compliance
docs.text: Support with NCA, SAMA, NIA, NISCF, QCB and GCC privacy requirements, combined with ISO 27001, business continuity and ongoing GRC support.

docs.title: Do these frameworks apply to foreign companies?
docs.text: It depends on the framework, your sector and whether you operate in the country or supply regulated entities there. Some requirements apply directly to regulated entities and are passed to their suppliers through contracts. We start by establishing what applies to you.

docs.title: Can ISO 27001 satisfy GCC regulatory requirements?
docs.text: ISO 27001 can provide a strong foundation and often overlaps significantly, but regulatory frameworks contain their own specific requirements. Mapping the two avoids duplicated work without assuming one replaces the other.

docs.title: Applicability review
docs.text: Establishing which frameworks apply to your organisation, and which your customers or regulators expect you to align with.

docs.title: Gap assessment
docs.text: Assessing current controls against the applicable regulatory requirements.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Developing the governance, policies and controls needed to close gaps.

docs.title: Evidence and reporting
docs.text: Establishing evidence and preparing for regulatory review or self-assessment where required.

docs.title: Standards integration
docs.text: Aligning regulatory controls with ISO 27001, ISO 22301 and privacy programmes.

docs.title: Ongoing governance
docs.text: GRC and vCISO support to keep compliance current.

docs.title: Cyber Essentials Readiness
docs.text: Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus readiness, remediation and submission support. Assessment is carried out by an authorised Certification Body.

docs.title: What is the difference between Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus?
docs.text: Cyber Essentials is a self-assessment verified by a Certification Body. Cyber Essentials Plus uses the same requirements but adds a hands-on technical audit of your systems by an assessor.

docs.title: How long is certification valid?
docs.text: Certification reflects your position at the time of assessment, and the scheme expects organisations to recertify at least every 12 months.

docs.title: Readiness assessment
docs.text: Establishing the scope and assessing your current position against the scheme requirements.

docs.title: Control review
docs.text: Reviewing configuration, patching, access control, malware protection and boundary controls.

docs.title: Gap identification
docs.text: Identifying where controls fall short of the requirements, prioritised for remediation.

docs.title: Remediation support
docs.text: Helping your team or IT provider address the gaps.

docs.title: Evidence and submission preparation
docs.text: Helping you prepare accurate answers and supporting evidence for the self-assessment.

docs.title: Certification Body coordination
docs.text: Coordinating with an authorised Certification Body for the assessment and, for Cyber Essentials Plus, the technical audit.
